processing: Fully oxidised black tea from a modernised factory, made largely from leaf supplied by local smallholders. Documented auction grades include OP1 and BOP1.
harvest_season: As with other low-grown Ceylon teas, plucking runs through much of the year rather than in fixed flushes. No single prized season is well documented for this estate.
appearance_dry: Long dark twisted leaf, with silvery tips in the better lots.
appearance_wet: Dark coppery-brown leaf, typical of a fully oxidised low-grown tea.
taste_profile: Sellers describe a sweet caramel note in a rounded, balanced cup. Low-grown Ceylon teas generally run fuller and softer than high-grown ones, with less sharp briskness.

brewing.notes: Usual Western brewing for a Ceylon leaf tea. Tippy grades are gentler, so start at the short end, and try the larger OP grades without milk first.

vintage_note: Sold by grade and lot rather than by vintage, through the Colombo auction and on to specialty shops. As with other Ceylon blacks, buy recent stock and drink it within a year or two. The grade name matters here, since a tippy lot and a plain OP from the same factory are very different purchases.
description:
New Vithanakande is a tea factory and estate south of Ratnapura in Sri Lanka, on the edge of the Sinharaja rainforest. At about 130 metres it sits at the very bottom of the island's tea country, and it is one of the names people give when arguing that low-grown Ceylon can be a fine tea and not only a blending base.

The tea depends on smallholders. One account puts the suppliers at around 6,500 small growers, some with plots the size of a vegetable garden. Its reputation is credited to a factory that was upgraded under the family that runs it.

The cup is described as ruby red with a sweet caramel side, balanced enough to drink all day. Treat it as a Western-brewed black: boiling or nearly boiling water and three to four minutes, shorter for the tippy grades.

When buying, look at the grade and the lot, because the name covers a wide range. What is documented is that its OP1 and BOP1 lots set record auction prices in the low-grown category in October 2019.
history:
A family owned the old Vithanakande factory and its gardens. Navaratne Pilapitiya, of that family, left a planter's job with an agency firm after a couple of years to take them over. He upgraded the factory, renamed it New Vithanakande, and developed smallholder gardens in the village of Delwala and then around Kalawana and beyond.

He chaired the Private Tea Factory Owners Association from 1999 to 2001. A tribute to him appeared in 2019, the year the press described the factory as owned by the family of the late Pilapitiya. The founding date of the original factory is not confirmed here.
